en: The Questions of King Milinda:
The Chapter on Similes, Section on the Lion (Sīhavagga)
2. The Question on the Cakravāka Bird “Venerable Nāgasena, as for what you say—that ‘three qualities of the cakravāka bird should be adopted’—which are those three qualities that should be adopted?
“Just as, Great King, the cakravāka does not abandon his mate until the end of his life;”
In the same way, Great King, a practitioner of yoga should not abandon wise attention until the end of life.
This, Great King, is the first quality of the ruddy sheldrake that should be adopted.
Furthermore, Great King, the ruddy sheldrake feeds on water-moss and algae, and he finds contentment therein; through that contentment, he does not decline in strength or in beauty.
In the same way, Great King, a yogi who is a practitioner of yoga should practice contentment with whatever is obtained.
For, Great King, a yogi who is a practitioner of yoga who is content with whatever is obtained does not decline in virtue,
does not decline in concentration, does not decline in wisdom, does not decline in liberation, and does not decline in the knowledge and vision of liberation.
He does not fall away from any wholesome states.
This, Great King, is the second quality of the ruddy goose that should be adopted.
Furthermore, Great King, the ruddy goose does not harm living beings.

In the same way, Great King, a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, should be one who has laid aside the rod, laid aside the weapon, who is modest, compassionate, and sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.
This, Great King, is the third quality to be adopted from the ruddy goose (*cakkavāka*).
And this, Great King, was spoken by the Blessed One, the God above gods, in the *Cakkavāka Jātaka*:
“He who neither kills nor causes to kill,
neither conquers nor causes to conquer,
whose heart is full of loving-kindness toward all beings— ”
"His truth cannot be contradicted by anyone.
Thus ends the second question, on the Cakkavāka bird.
